paragraphs: Comparing distributions requires balancing sensitivity to meaningful differences against resistance to unusual observations. The 2-Wasserstein distance captures small geometric changes, but a small amount of outlier mass can make otherwise similar distributions appear very different. Sampling discrepancies also make its empirical estimates converge relatively slowly in the two-dimensional setting studied here.

The paper introduces k-RPW, a family of distances built from partial transport between distributions. The authors prove that these distances satisfy the requirements of a metric while resisting small outlier masses and retaining sensitivity to minor geometric differences. For constant k and samples in two dimensions, the stated convergence rate improves from n to the power of −1/4 to n to the power of −1/3.

The construction extends from partial 2-Wasserstein transport to general p-Wasserstein transport. Appropriate parameter settings recover several established distances, connecting them within one family. Experiments on noisy image retrieval datasets report higher accuracy than 1-Wasserstein, 2-Wasserstein, and total variation distances, supporting the usefulness of combining geometric sensitivity with outlier robustness.
icml-2024-a-new-robust-partial-p-wassers.tldr: The paper develops distribution distances that resist small outlier masses while preserving geometric sensitivity and improving stated sampling convergence rates.

paragraphs: Quantization makes large language models more compact, while LoRA provides a way to fine-tune them. Combining the two can support deployment on constrained hardware, but the paper argues that existing approaches can lose enough information to severely reduce accuracy. In some cases, LoRA fine-tuning then fails to deliver its intended benefit.

IR-QLoRA addresses this problem through two components organized around information retention. Information Calibration Quantization uses parameter statistics to preserve information during quantization. Information Elastic Connection changes how LoRA transforms representations during fine-tuning, allowing it to use more diverse information. The approach therefore addresses both the compressed model parameters and the adaptation process that operates alongside them.

Experiments on LLaMA and LLaMA2 models report accuracy improvements at widths of two to four bits. For four-bit LLaMA-7B, the reported MMLU improvement is 1.4% over leading methods, with 0.31% additional time consumption. Compatibility with NormalFloat and Integer quantization suggests that the proposed components can improve accuracy across more than one quantization framework.
icml-2024-accurate-lora-finetuning-quant.tldr: IR-QLoRA improves quantized language-model fine-tuning by preserving information in both quantized parameters and LoRA representation transformations.

paragraphs: The paper examines a weakness in value-based reinforcement learning despite its strong sample efficiency. The authors find that these methods can make limited use of available knowledge early in training and can be sensitive to bias. Their focus is on improving how the agent chooses actions during learning, particularly when its learned values are still developing.

The proposed approach adds hypotheses to the decision process. A hypothesis is a limited description of the environment that gives the agent additional guidance. The method relies on these hypotheses being accurate and combines them with incremental learning to build a policy that is ready to adapt. ALH is the algorithm developed around this combination of descriptive guidance and policy adaptation.

The authors analyze a representative learning scheme and evaluate ALH on a varied collection of MuJoCo benchmarks. They report significant improvements over value-based methods and other strong baselines. These findings support using accurate environmental hypotheses to improve decisions, with the accuracy of that guidance remaining an explicit requirement of the approach.
icml-2024-augmenting-decision-with-hypot.tldr: ALH combines accurate environmental hypotheses with incremental policy learning to improve reinforcement-learning decisions and reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Spurious features correlate with training labels without providing the intended basis for prediction. They are often assumed to be easier to learn than core features, but that assumption leaves their relative complexity insufficiently examined. This paper studies how both complexity and correlation strength shape the process of learning, rather than examining only final predictive performance.

The authors develop a theoretical framework and synthetic dataset using Boolean function analysis. This gives them fine control over how difficult spurious features are relative to core features and how strongly they correlate with labels. In their study, simpler or more strongly correlated spurious features slow core-feature learning. Separate subnetworks learn the two feature types, but their learning periods can overlap.

The study also finds that spurious features persist after core features have been learned. This helps explain why retraining the final layer can work and exposes limitations of debiasing methods that depend on an early, distinct spurious-learning phase. Theoretical support specifically covers XOR features learned by a one-hidden-layer ReLU network.
icml-2024-complexity-matters-feature-lea.tldr: Controlled experiments and theory show how spurious-feature complexity and correlation strength affect core-feature learning and the assumptions behind debiasing methods.

paragraphs: Dense linear layers consume much of the computation in foundation models. This paper investigates replacing their matrices with structured alternatives that can use computation more efficiently. A central finding is that these alternatives need different initialization scales and learning rates, so their performance depends strongly on how they are trained, especially as model size increases.

Using ideas from Maximal Update Parameterization, the authors determine appropriate scaling for initialization and learning rates. They then compare how performance improves with additional computation across matrix structures. Their proposed Block Tensor-Train family includes Monarch matrices and provides a broader set of structured replacements for dense layers.

Across multiple tasks, Block Tensor-Train performs better at the same computational budget. On augmented CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, it yields exponentially lower training loss for the studied MLPs and vision transformers. On ImageNet-1k, it matches dense ViT-S/32 performance using 3.8 times less computation, and it also improves efficiency when training small GPT-2 models. The results connect structural choices with the training scales needed to realize their advantages.
icml-2024-compute-better-spent-replacing.tldr: Properly scaled structured matrix layers, especially Block Tensor-Train layers, improve performance per unit of computation across the studied vision and language tasks.

paragraphs: A model trained on labeled data from one domain can perform poorly when deployed in another. When unlabeled target-domain data is available, self-supervised pretraining can help build useful representations. However, the authors find that ordinary fine-tuning after pretraining does not consistently improve target-domain error over training directly on the labeled source data.

Connect Later changes the fine-tuning stage by introducing augmentations designed with knowledge of the distribution shift. Its motivating division of work is that pretraining learns useful representations within each domain, while targeted fine-tuning strengthens generalization between domains. This makes the choice of augmentation during adaptation a central part of obtaining value from pretraining.

The framework achieves reported state-of-the-art out-of-distribution accuracy on four tasks covering wildlife identification, tumor detection, and astronomy. It maintains comparable or better accuracy within the source distribution. These findings support targeted augmentation as a way to improve robustness in the studied domain-adaptation setting, where unlabeled target data and knowledge of the shift inform the approach.
icml-2024-connect-later-improving-fine-t.tldr: Connect Later uses shift-aware augmentations during fine-tuning to improve cross-domain generalization after self-supervised pretraining.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems combine many individual preference functions into a single objective. When there are millions of components, optimizing their combination can be computationally expensive. Centralizing them can also be inappropriate when the functions encode private preferences. This paper studies a federated setting in which clients retain their own functions while collaborating to maximize a weighted sum.

The authors adapt the continuous greedy algorithm to this arrangement. Clients take small local steps in parallel, and a central server aggregates their changes. To reduce the cost of involving many clients, each aggregation uses only a sampled subset. Communication is further reduced by allowing several local steps between aggregation rounds.

The theoretical result shows that the algorithm still provides a good approximate solution despite client subsampling and intermittent communication. Thus, those cost reductions come with an approximation guarantee in the studied setting. The paper also explains how the federated formulation applies to Maximum Coverage and Facility Location, connecting the method to fundamental discrete optimization problems.
icml-2024-decomposable-submodular-maximi.tldr: A federated continuous greedy algorithm retains approximation guarantees while reducing communication through local updates and client subsampling.

paragraphs: Networked dynamical systems describe cascading processes such as the spread of information or disease. Earlier learning results considered systems whose underlying network has a single layer. This paper examines multilayer networks, which offer a richer representation of such processes but make the task of inferring an unknown system more challenging.

The authors present an efficient algorithm with probably approximately correct learning guarantees. In this framework, the aim is to learn an accurate approximation with high probability from training examples. Their result shows that the unknown systems considered can be learned with a small number of examples, establishing that the added network structure remains compatible with efficient, theoretically supported learning.

The paper also analyzes the Natarajan dimension, a measure of the complexity of the model class. Its asymptotic bound is tight for almost all multilayer graphs. This complements the learning algorithm by characterizing the complexity underlying the problem, giving future studies a theoretical basis for investigating learning over multilayer dynamical systems.
icml-2024-efficient-pac-learnability-of-.tldr: The paper establishes efficient PAC learning for multilayer network dynamics and tightly characterizes model complexity for almost all multilayer graphs.

paragraphs: Reaching a goal safely creates two difficulties for reinforcement learning: safety rules can terminate exploration, and goal-based rewards can be sparse. Restricting exploration to safe regions addresses only part of the problem. An agent can still spend substantial effort on safe behavior that does not help it reach its goal.

The paper introduces a feasible reachable function that describes whether some policy can reach the goal safely within a finite time horizon. This function obeys a self-consistency condition and a risky Bellman equation, enabling its computation through fixed-point iteration. It provides a way to narrow the search using both safety and goal reachability.

Feasible reachable policy iteration combines policy evaluation, region expansion, and policy improvement. During region expansion, information about reaching the goal accelerates convergence of the feasible region and identifies a smaller feasible reachable region. Experiments report faster convergence to comparable or better performance without sacrificing safety, together with higher sample efficiency. The findings support using goal information to make safe exploration more productive.
icml-2024-feasible-reachable-policy-iter.tldr: FRPI narrows reinforcement-learning exploration using both safety and finite-horizon goal reachability, improving convergence and sample efficiency in experiments.

paragraphs: Federated fine-tuning allows language models to learn from data held on end devices. Updating every model parameter could offer benefits beyond parameter-efficient tuning, but exchanging the associated information is expensive for billion-parameter models. This paper targets that communication barrier so that full-parameter tuning becomes feasible in the federated setting.

FedKSeed uses zeroth-order optimization with a finite collection of random seeds. Communication between clients and the server consists of a few seeds and scalar gradient quantities, reducing transmitted information to a few thousand bytes. The authors also introduce unequal sampling probabilities for seeds, giving priority to perturbations with a greater effect on model accuracy.

Experiments span six scenarios with different language models, datasets, and data partitions. The method outperforms the compared federated fine-tuning approaches in communication efficiency and zero-shot generalization. The findings show that sharply reducing the information exchanged need not prevent effective full-parameter adaptation in these evaluations, and that choosing which perturbations to emphasize can further support the approach.
icml-2024-federated-full-parameter-tunin.tldr: FedKSeed enables federated full-parameter language-model tuning by communicating random seeds and scalar gradient quantities instead of large parameter updates.

paragraphs: A covariance matrix summarizes how different dimensions of data vary together. This paper considers estimating that matrix when the information is split between two collaborating agents. Each agent observes a separate set of dimensions from the same collection of samples, and both must send limited-bit messages to a central server that constructs the estimate.

The authors analyze how estimation accuracy depends jointly on the number of dimensions, the number of samples, and the communication budget. They prove a lower bound on the error achievable by any estimator in this setting. That bound identifies a fundamental restriction imposed by the available data and communication, rather than a shortcoming of one particular estimation method.

The paper then supplies an algorithm whose error matches the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor. Pairing an achievable result with an impossibility bound makes the near-optimality claim meaningful: the proposed procedure approaches the best accuracy permitted by the studied distributed setup. The contribution characterizes how communication constraints enter an otherwise statistical estimation problem.
icml-2024-fundamental-limits-of-distribu.tldr: The paper bounds the best possible covariance-estimation accuracy under limited communication and gives an algorithm that approaches that bound.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization learns how to improve an objective through function evaluations rather than direct gradient access. In high dimensions, estimating useful gradients can require many queries. This paper studies nonconvex functions whose gradients are approximately sparse, meaning their important information is concentrated in relatively few coordinates.

The proposed Gradient Compressed Sensing estimator, GraCe, reduces the per-step query requirement from order s log(d/s) to order s log log(d/s), while retaining the stated order 1/T convergence rate over T steps. Here, d is the dimension and s describes gradient sparsity. The estimator extends the Indyk–Price–Woodruff compressed-sensing algorithm from linear measurements to nonlinear functions.

The authors also address the large constant that makes the original compressed-sensing procedure impractical. Their dependent random partition technique and analysis reduce that constant by nearly a factor of 4,300. On 10,000-dimensional functions, GraCe significantly outperforms 12 compared zeroth-order methods. The contribution combines improved dimensional dependence with changes aimed at making the theoretical approach empirically useful.
icml-2024-gradient-compressed-sensing-a-.tldr: GraCe exploits approximately sparse gradients to reduce high-dimensional optimization queries while preserving the stated convergence rate.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter optimization can consume substantial computation because candidate configurations require training. Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization allocates resources incrementally across configurations, using partial learning curves to guide further investment. Its predictive surrogate must be updated frequently, however, and online retraining or fine-tuning can add overhead, instability, and another layer of settings to manage.

FT-PFN replaces those repeated neural-surrogate updates with in-context prediction. This prior-data fitted network uses a transformer's ability to condition on supplied observations to extrapolate learning curves through Bayesian prediction in a single forward pass. The aim is to make the predictions needed for incremental resource allocation both fast and reliable.

Across three benchmark suites, FT-PFN provides more accurate predictions and is 10–100 times faster than the deep Gaussian process and deep ensemble surrogates used in previous work. Combined with the authors' MFPI-random acquisition mechanism, it forms ifBO, which achieves reported state-of-the-art results in those benchmark families. The findings connect better surrogate predictions with improved decisions about where to spend training resources.
icml-2024-in-context-freeze-thaw-bayesia.tldr: FT-PFN predicts learning curves in one forward pass, enabling faster surrogate updates and stronger freeze-thaw hyperparameter optimization in the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Inverse constrained reinforcement learning aims to infer safety constraints as well as control policies. Many existing methods assume ongoing access to an interactive environment for extensive data collection. That assumption is difficult to satisfy when collecting more experience is dangerous or costly, motivating a method that learns from offline demonstrations.

ICSDICE estimates superior distributions and extracts feasible constraints from them. These distributions emphasize policies with the capacity to achieve rewards beyond those of the expert. The method estimates them through a regularized dual optimization problem, drawing on both observed reward signals and expert preferences to guide safe control.

The approach encourages sparsity and accounts for discounting within its learned and observed distributions, with the goals of obtaining transferable constraints and unbiased estimates. Empirical studies report better constraint recovery than the compared baselines and successful adaptation to high-dimensional environments. The contribution is an offline route to learning constraints while seeking reward-improving policies, reducing reliance on the interactive sampling assumed by earlier approaches.
icml-2024-learning-constraints-from-offl.tldr: ICSDICE learns safety constraints from offline demonstrations using reward signals and expert preferences to identify promising feasible policies.

paragraphs: Predicting phenotypes from fMRI depends on identifying informative relationships among brain regions. Pairwise connections can miss relationships involving larger groups. The paper proposes seeking group relationships that provide as much useful information as possible while repeating as little information as possible, a principle the authors call maximally informative and minimally redundant.

HyBRiD represents these relationships using hyperedges, which can connect multiple brain regions at once. A Constructor identifies hyperedge structures, and a Weighter assigns their weights. This design avoids searching the full exponential collection of possible group relationships. A multi-head drop-bottleneck framework supplies a tractable route to the information objective, together with theoretical guarantees.

Experiments support the effectiveness of the resulting relationships. The authors report an average 11.2% improvement over the state-of-the-art predictive model in hyperedge quality measured through the CPM protocol. This finding concerns the informativeness of learned brain connections under that evaluation. The approach makes higher-order relationship discovery computationally manageable while explicitly accounting for redundant information among the relationships it learns.
icml-2024-learning-high-order-relationsh.tldr: HyBRiD learns informative, minimally redundant groups of brain-region relationships from fMRI without exhaustively searching all possible groups.

paragraphs: Causal inference algorithms can identify which causal questions are answerable from a causal structure and data. Applying them to high-dimensional variables such as images is difficult because accurately estimating the required distributions is impractical. Deep generative models can produce samples from such distributions, but training them can itself be expensive.

Modular-DCM addresses this problem through modular training that can incorporate large pretrained conditional generative models. Given the causal structure, it uses adversarial training to learn network weights. The authors establish that the method can provably sample from identifiable causal queries even when latent confounders are present. The guarantee is specifically about identifiable queries and presupposes the supplied causal structure.

Experiments on Colored-MNIST show improvements over the compared baselines. Additional results demonstrate convergence on COVIDx and usefulness for a causal invariant prediction problem on CelebA-HQ. Together, these results support modular generative modeling as a way to connect high-dimensional data generation with causal inference while reusing pretrained components to improve learning efficiency.
icml-2024-modular-learning-of-deep-causa.tldr: Modular-DCM reuses pretrained generative components to support provable sampling from identifiable causal queries given a causal structure, including settings with latent confounders.

paragraphs: Structure-based molecular generation seeks molecules that bind well to a target, but favorable binding scores are less useful when the generated three-dimensional pose is infeasible. The paper investigates why autoregressive and diffusion approaches can produce problematic conformations. Its analysis examines mode collapse and the difficulty of combining continuous and discrete spaces.

MolCRAFT moves the generation process into a continuous parameter space and introduces a sampling strategy designed to reduce noise. This approach addresses the representation and sampling choices underlying molecular geometry. The aim is to generate molecules that combine strong binding affinity with more stable three-dimensional structures, accounting for the interactions between atoms.

Empirical results report improvements in both binding affinity and structural stability. MolCRAFT reaches a reference-level Vina score of −6.59 kcal/mol at comparable molecular size, with a reported −0.84 kcal/mol margin over strong baselines. These results support the proposed representation and sampling strategy for generating promising molecular poses, with the stated evidence centered on computational binding scores and generated structures.
icml-2024-molcraft-structure-based-drug-.tldr: MolCRAFT generates molecules in continuous parameter space to improve both binding scores and the stability of generated three-dimensional structures.

paragraphs: When an outcome's distribution changes between two samples, several underlying mechanisms may have contributed. This paper asks how to quantify each mechanism's contribution when multiple explanatory variables are involved. The method starts from a given causal model, which supplies the structure needed to interpret the observed change in causal terms.

The proposed estimator combines regression with reweighting. Its defining property is multiple robustness: it can recover the target quantity despite partial model misspecification. This gives the procedure tolerance to certain modeling errors. The authors also prove consistency and asymptotic normality, establishing that the estimator approaches its target and has a characterized distribution in large samples.

The estimator can be incorporated into attribution frameworks such as Shapley values, which inherit these statistical properties. Monte Carlo simulations show strong performance, and an empirical application illustrates its usefulness. An implementation is included in DoWhy. The contribution is a statistically supported way to estimate causal contributions that can fit within existing attribution workflows.
icml-2024-multiply-robust-causal-change-.tldr: A regression-and-reweighting estimator attributes distribution changes to causal mechanisms while retaining validity under partial model misspecification.

paragraphs: Deploying an updated reinforcement-learning policy can be expensive, making frequent policy changes undesirable even when more interaction data can be collected. This paper studies multi-agent learning under limits on adaptivity. Its main setting is a two-player zero-sum Markov game, where the objective is to learn effectively while requiring few policy-update batches.

The authors design a policy-elimination algorithm with regret bounded by approximately the square root of H³S²ABK, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here, H is the horizon, S the number of states, A and B the players' action counts, and K the number of episodes. Its batch complexity grows only as H plus log log K, allowing interaction to scale with very slowly increasing update requirements.

A lower bound shows that algorithms achieving square-root-in-K regret cannot arbitrarily reduce batch complexity. It matches the proposed upper bound up to logarithmic factors, supporting near-optimality of the update schedule. The techniques also extend to bandit games and reward-free multi-agent learning with near-optimal batch complexity.
icml-2024-near-optimal-reinforcement-lea.tldr: A policy-elimination method achieves strong regret guarantees in two-player zero-sum games with nearly the minimum required number of policy-update batches.

paragraphs: Large batches have empirically helped differentially private stochastic gradient descent, but the reasons have lacked a clear theoretical account. This paper studies the variability in gradient updates to explain that behavior. It separates total gradient variance into one component caused by subsampling data and another caused by the noise used for privacy.

The authors prove that, in the limit of infinitely many iterations, effective noise-induced variance does not depend on batch size. The subsampling component, however, decreases as batches grow. Consequently, larger batches reduce effective total gradient variance in this regime even though the effective privacy-noise component remains unchanged.

Numerical results indicate that this limiting analysis is relevant to practical settings when batches are not small. Outside that regime, the authors observe an even greater reduction in total variance with larger batches. They also derive a sufficient condition under which larger batches reduce effective privacy-noise variance for a single iteration. That one-step conclusion is conditional, complementing the separate long-run result.
icml-2024-subsampling-is-not-magic-why-l.tldr: The paper explains large-batch benefits in DP-SGD by separating sampling variance from privacy-noise variance and analyzing their batch-size dependence.

paragraphs: Temperature affects how foundation models use their scores. In language models, it rescales logits before softmax for next-token generation; in CLIP training, it rescales similarities within the contrastive loss. This paper asks whether a small neural network can predict a useful temperature for each input, making temperature selection responsive to the data.

The proposed TempNet is paired with a learning framework based on constrained distributionally robust optimization. That framework supplies robust losses, while theoretical considerations inform the network design. TempNet can be trained jointly with a foundation model from scratch or learned separately for an already pretrained model, giving it two routes into existing modeling workflows.

The authors report that the learned temperature predictor generalizes and transfers to new tasks. Experiments with both language models and CLIP show substantial improvements over existing solutions or models. These findings support input-specific temperature prediction as a useful learned component across the evaluated settings, linking a small auxiliary network to consequential choices in foundation-model training and inference.
icml-2024-to-cool-or-not-to-cool-tempera.tldr: TempNet learns input-specific temperatures through a distributionally robust framework, improving the evaluated language and CLIP models.

paragraphs: Using pretrained weights to initialize a downstream model ties that model to the pretrained architecture, which may be too large for economical deployment. It also makes combining complementary knowledge from several pretrained models difficult. This paper studies how to transfer useful knowledge into smaller, task-specific models while allowing their architectures to be chosen independently.

Adaptive Feature Transfer operates on features rather than weights. It selectively transfers the pretrained features most useful for the downstream task through a simple regularization term with minimal overhead. This task-dependent selection avoids treating every pretrained feature as equally valuable and allows knowledge from multiple models to contribute to one downstream learner.

Across vision, language, and multimodal datasets, AFT improves downstream performance over alternatives with similar computational cost. Improvements in the pretrained models also translate reliably into downstream gains, including when the downstream model is more than 50 times smaller. The reported results further show effective transfer of complementary information from multiple pretrained models, supporting flexible reuse of foundation-model knowledge.
icml-2024-transferring-knowledge-from-la.tldr: Adaptive Feature Transfer selectively moves task-relevant features from large pretrained models into smaller models with independently chosen architectures.

paragraphs: Inaccurate supervision can take different annotation forms, leading researchers to develop separate methods for each one. ULAREF starts from a shared property: even inaccurate annotations retain some correct labeling information. The paper uses that commonality to build a unified framework that improves the labels used to train a predictive model.

The framework combines global reliability detection with local label enhancement. It first identifies which labeling information is unreliable, then uses an enhanced model to help refine it. This enhanced model is fine-tuned with a proposed consistency loss. The predictive model learns from the resulting refined labels, connecting reliability assessment directly to the supervision it receives.

The authors theoretically justify a key part of this process: under mild assumptions, the enhanced model can be more accurate than the predictive model on the detected unreliable subset. This conditional result supports using the enhanced model where label correction is needed. The contribution is a common refinement strategy for different inaccurate-supervision forms, with theory explaining why its local enhancement can help.
icml-2024-ularef-a-unified-label-refinem.tldr: ULAREF unifies learning from inaccurate annotations by detecting unreliable labels and refining them with a consistency-trained enhanced model.

paragraphs: Concept-based models explain predictions using concepts people can understand. Human reasoning also uses relationships among concepts, raising a further question: do these models represent those relationships correctly? This paper examines the internal concept representations learned by such models, extending the analysis beyond whether individual concepts can appear in an explanation.

The authors empirically find that the studied state-of-the-art models learn representations that lack stability and robustness and fail to capture relationships among concepts. These results identify a weakness in the structure of their explanations: having human-understandable concept labels does not by itself establish that the model has learned how those concepts relate to one another.

The paper then introduces an algorithm that uses inter-concept relationships to improve concept intervention accuracy. Interventions allow changes at the concept level to affect the model's behavior, making this a practical test of the value of relational information. The reported improvement demonstrates that correctly accounting for relationships can benefit downstream tasks, linking the analysis of representation quality to an actionable modeling improvement.
icml-2024-understanding-inter-concept-re.tldr: The paper finds weaknesses in learned concept relationships and shows that using those relationships can improve concept intervention accuracy.

paragraphs: Linear attention promises efficient sequence processing, but implementation details can prevent that advantage from appearing in practice. The paper identifies cumulative summation operations as a bottleneck in previous implementations. Lightning Attention addresses it and is reported to maintain constant training speed across sequence lengths under fixed memory consumption.

The method divides attention into computations within blocks and computations between blocks. It uses conventional attention inside each block and linear-attention kernel techniques across blocks, removing the need for cumulative summation in the linear calculation. Tiling in both the forward and backward passes further adapts the computation to GPU hardware.

The authors also introduce TransNormerLLM, an architecture designed around Lightning Attention to preserve efficiency while improving accuracy. Evaluations use standard and self-collected datasets across different model sizes and sequence lengths. The resulting models are more efficient than the compared language models while achieving benchmark performance comparable to leading conventional transformers. These findings connect the attention implementation to a complete architecture that realizes the reported efficiency benefits.
icml-2024-various-lengths-constant-speed.tldr: Lightning Attention combines within-block and between-block computations to deliver constant reported training speed across sequence lengths at fixed memory consumption.
